comparator.sourceNotes: The official year pages itemize 60+60+60=180 EC. Year one consists of 60 EC compulsory orientation, academic/professional formation, dental knowledge, medical–dental interaction and two preclinical dental components. Year two has 57 EC compulsory professional formation, dental knowledge, medical–dental interaction, preclinical training and the 7-EC Bachelor Clinic, plus a genuinely unrestricted 3-EC elective. Radboud specifies supervised patient treatment beginning in the second semester. Year three has 60 EC compulsory academic/professional and research work, dental knowledge, medical–dental interaction, preclinical training, an 11-EC third-year clinic and pain. The year-three page says students work on a bachelor thesis, and itemizes a 10.5-EC research/formation component but no separate thesis line; no additional thesis credits have been invented. The publicly listed year pages do not identify a prospective academic year and should not be treated as a fixed entrant-cohort contract. routeSelection.route: Ordinary three-year Dentistry bachelor including preclinical and supervised patient treatment
routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Dentistry bachelor; its official three-year year pages give one ordinary 180-EC route. Only the genuinely open 3-EC year-two choice is left unfilled.

core: Medical and biological foundations of oral health: cells, physiology, anatomy, biochemistry, immunity, pathology and pharmacology
Disease mechanisms, diagnosis, prevention and treatment as scientific questions
Scientific inquiry, epidemiology, evidence evaluation and biomedical research
Psychological and social dimensions of oral health, patient experience and health behaviour
Communication, interdisciplinary teamwork and leadership in oral healthcare
Professional clinical dentistry and supervised patient treatment
Preclinical procedures, manual precision, radiology and dental technical skills
Ethics, patient rights and professional responsibility in health research and care
questions: How do biological processes produce oral health and disease?
How do behaviour, communication and social conditions shape prevention and patient care?
How can health evidence support prevention, diagnosis and treatment decisions?

alternatives.label: Biomedical science, oral health & disease
alternatives.labelReason: Eleven life-science and biomedical courses, four research and epidemiology courses, and complementary psychology, ethics and law courses make biomedical oral-health questions the programme centre. The label avoids implying dental training or qualification.
alternatives.concept: Study the biological and medical foundations relevant to oral health through cell biology, biochemistry, physiology, anatomy, neurobiology, pharmacology, immunity, pathology, epidemiology, laboratory work and evidence synthesis. This is a related-fields response to Dentistry: it does not teach dental anatomy, restorative materials and procedures, radiology, preclinical dental technique or supervised treatment of patients.
progression: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine precedes all advanced life-science and biomedical courses; Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes advanced psychology and cognition. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods and the Advanced Research Seminar. All formal prerequisites and exact planned offerings pass; ten courses are at 300 level.

alternatives.label: Health psychology, communication & patient-centred care
alternatives.labelReason: Eight psychology and neuroscience courses plus leadership, communication, sociology, ethics, law, epidemiology and research methods make patient behaviour and collaborative care the organising centre; the label does not claim clinical dentistry.
alternatives.concept: Study psychological and social influences on health behaviour, patient experience and decision-making, together with communication, leadership, teamwork, diversity, ethics, epidemiology and research methods. This route responds to Dentistry’s behavioural, social and team-care strands but provides no dental diagnosis, procedures, clinical communication training or supervised patient treatment.
alternatives.distinctness: The first route is organised around biomedical mechanisms of health and disease. The second replaces ten molecular, anatomical, physiological, immunological and laboratory courses with social psychology, leadership, communication, sociology, qualitative research, AI ethics and behavioural decision-making. Each route therefore has 75 EC not present in the other, above the 30-EC floor.
progression: Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes advanced psychology and cognition, while Research Methods & Statistics precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods, organisational psychology, diversity leadership and behavioural economics. Introductory sociology, psychology, leadership and communication precede advanced qualitative, persuasive and organisational work. All formal prerequisites and exact planned offerings pass; eight courses are at 300 level.

candidates.label: Clinical dentistry, preclinical procedures & technical treatment
candidates.assessment: UCR has no dental simulation, oral examination, radiology, restorative-materials teaching, manual dental procedures or supervised dental clinic. No complete programme can implement this professional-clinical direction without relabelling general biomedical and psychology courses as dental training.

selection.assessment: The historical judgment correctly identified the absence of dental and clinical training but treated that absence as excluding any complete UCR response. A biomedical oral-health route and a distinct health-psychology and communication route are coherent, evidence-backed and mechanically feasible, and differ by ten courses each. The next candidate is the defining clinical and preclinical dentistry direction; UCR cannot implement it, so production stops at two and preserves that limitation explicitly.

notes.text: Radboud Dentistry combines dental theory, preclinical technical training, radiology, behavioural and medical science, supervised patient treatment and professional formation. UCR can build coherent programmes around biomedical oral-health questions or the psychological, communicative and social dimensions of care, but neither programme teaches dentistry, offers dental procedures or patient treatment, or leads toward qualification as a dentist.

The required Radboud preclinical and clinic sequence has no UCR counterpart. UCR biomedical, psychology, communication and leadership courses are shown only as related academic study; they are not substitutes for oral examination, dental radiology, restorative materials and procedures, manual dental technique or supervised clinical care.
